# Introduction

01/26/90 (11:36)

Like many other American fathers that chose a mate and started out on the adventure of life, taking care of this girl whom you love above all others on this earth is a very serious and full-time job. It is, perhaps, not as serious or time-consuming as bearing children and raising them, but the female of this relationship has a God-given compensation for her years of constant nurturing and devotion; she watches her children grow up and evolve into complex adults, a combination of both of our genes and yet so individual that it has been said, "There is not another person on earth exactly like you." What a wonderful and fulfilling experience that must be!

As the years go by, which they seem to do ever more rapidly, you seem to be dimly aware that something is missing. Eventually, the many, many times over the years when your mate has warned you that "Your children are growing up and you are missing it!" sinks in and you realize that, as usual, your mate's warnings were true, but this "serious business" that has engrossed you over the past four decades, this business of providing the very best of material things for your loved ones, has cost you a terrible price. It had to be paid and yet you have often wondered if it was worth it. Your answer was always, "Yes." Giving life your "best shot" is the only way to go. Your wife trusted you to give your best just as she has always done. So you devoted yourself to giving your loved ones the best you could afford in this very material world.

But the price had to be paid.......and it was. My children grew up and are now no longer children. They are all adults. What happened? Where did the years go to? They never wanted for anything......except a father that would bounce them on his knee, play with them, tuck them in at night and teach them about God.

The purpose of this book, then, is to try and make up for all the years when there just wasn't enough hours in a day, or you were too tired, or the children were asleep when you got home. It can't, of course, but it is an attempt to share with my children some of the things and answers I have learned over the past lifetime in the hope that it will make their lives happier or better or more understandable.........a small, futile token to make up for the years when they never saw much of their father and yet these writings are dedicated with love and hope that they will somehow, someday understand.

Also included in this book you will find many of the things that I have collected during the course of a rather somber childhood and uneventful adult life. Things which I have treasured over the years and finally compiled them under one cover. They also are offered with much love and the hope that you also will treasure them and read them occasionally when the need arises.

C.E.A.

# Preface

In the Song Of Bernadette it is stated so beautifully,

> To those who understood,
> no explanation is necessary---
> To those who do not understand,
> no explanation is possible.

How many times in your life have you tried to explain something to someone, and they just couldn't grasp what you were trying to say? How many times have you heard people, in a bar for instance, vociferously expounding on a subject of which it was apparent to many in the room that he or she knew very little of the actual subject? How many times have you been enjoying a cultural subject such as good art,classical music, poetry, or a thoughtful discussion with a friend about philosophy, religion, economics, politics or some other subject when nearby people will make derogatory remarks about the subject? This happened to me many, many times and it still does. Using clasical music as an illustration, for instance, you think to yourself, "How can anyone deride classical music. It has lasted for hundreds of years and will doubtless last forever. It was created by masters who had more creativity and genius in their little toe than the people who were sneering or ridiculing classical music."

Up until a few years ago, these people always annoyed me and my blood pressure would doubtless rise because of it. And then, one day while reading a Science Of Mind Magazine, I ran across the above quotation and it literally changed my life.
It is one of the most important things I have ever read and deserves much thought, consideration and even meditation. It explained so much about people to me. After many years, the pieces of the puzzle of life started to come together.

The reason we have spent so much time talking about the above quotation is that this "book" will be full of "hints" and "goodies" but they will only be recognized as such or be of use to you if you realize that they are there. If you don't understand, make an effort. It can change your life for the better...............

# The Greatest Commandment

## Matthew 22

36 Master, which is the greatest commandment in the law?

37 Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.

38 This is the first and greatest commandment.

39 And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.

40 On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.

## MATTHEW 7

12 Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.

Life is really very simple and very beautiful. It doesn't have to be complicated and unattractive. Each day can be an adventure of harmony, personal satisfaction and happiness. All you have to do is to keep life uncomplicated. If you live by the Greatest Commandment and the Golden Rule, that is all that is necessary to guarantee you a life of fulfillment and happiness.

This does not mean that you will win the lottery and become a sudden millionaire. It does not mean that you will have material wealth. In fact, it doesn't have anything to do with material possessions. It has only to do with our life and how you feel inside.

If you will but follow these two simple commandments each day, all day long, day-after-day, your life will soon change for the better. None will notice it at first, except you. But as these two simple things become you, you and your life will change.

Most people think that if I only had good looks, or was smarter, or had a new car, or a better job, or more money, then I would be happy. But this is not so. If it were so, millionaires or movie stars would be the only truly happy people. Those who were as handsome as Alan Ladd or as beautiful as Marilyn Monroe would be the happiest of all. (Incidentally, they both committed suicide!) You can see that material things have nothing to do with true happiness.

Generally, people have a tendency to look for happiness everywhere but where it actually is.......within you. When you learn to live by these two simple, basic tenets, you will experience what true happiness really is. This is no idle promise. It has been proven millions of times already all over this earth. It cannot fail. Try it! What have you got to lose? Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind.---Love your neighbor as much as you love yourself---Do for others

what you want them to do for you. It won't be easy at first, but the reward is well worth the effort!

# If

If you can keep your head when all about you  
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you,  
If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you,  
But make allowance for their doubting too;  
If you can wait and not be tired by waiting,  
Or being lied about, don't deal in lies,  
Or being hated don't give way to hating,  
And yet don't look too good, nor talk too wise:

If you can dream-- and not make dreams your master;  
If you can think-- and not make thoughts your aim,  
If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster  
And treat those two impostors just the same;  
If you can bear to hear the truth you've spoken  
Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools,  
Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken,  
And stoop and build 'em up with worn-out tools:

If you can make one heap of all your winnings  
And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss,  
And lose, and start again at your beginnings  
And never breathe a word about your loss;  
If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew  
To serve your turn long after they are gone,  
And so hold on when there is nothing in you  
Except the Will which says to them: "Hold on!"

If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,  
Or walk with Kings--nor lose the common touch,  
If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,  
If all men count with you, but none too much;  
If you can fill the unforgiving minute  
With sixty seconds' worth of distance run,  
Yours is the Earth and everything that's in it,  
And--which is more--you'll be a man, my son!

Rudyard Kipling

# The Power of the Dog

There is sorrow enough in the natural way
From men and women to fill our day;
And when we are certain of sorrow in store,
Why do we always arrange for more?
Brothers and Sisters, I bid you beware
Of giving your heart to a dog to tear.

Buy a pup and your money will buy
Love unflinching that cannot lie--
Perfect passion and worship fed
By a kick in the ribs or a pat on the head.
Nevertheless it is hardly fair
To risk your heart for a dog to tear.

When the fourteen years which Nature permits
Are closing in asthma, or tumour, or fits,
To lethal chambers or loaded guns,
Then you will find--it's your own affair--
But . . . . you've given your heart to a dog to tear.

When the body that lived at your single will,
With its whimper of welcome, is stilled (how still!),
When the spirit that answered your every mood
Is gone--wherever it goes--for good,
You will discover how much you care,
And will give your heart to a dog to tear.

We've sorrow enough in the natural way,
When it comes to Christian clay.
Our loves are not given, but only lent,
At compound interest of cent per cent.
Though it is not always the case, I believe,
That the longer we've kept 'em, the more do we grieve:
For, when debts are payable, right or wrong,
A short-time loan is as bad as a long--
So why in--Heaven (before we are there)
Should we give our hearts to a dog to tear?

Rudyard Kipling

# The Female of the Species

1911

When the Himalayan peasant meets the he-bear in his pride,
He shouts to scare the monster, who will often turn aside,
But the she-bear thus accosted rends the peasant tooth and nail,
For the female of the species is more deadly than the male.

When Nag the basking cobra hears the careless foot of man,
He will sometimes wriggle sideways and avoid it if he can.
But his mate makes no such motion where she camps beside the trail,
For the female of the species is more deadly than the male.

When the early Jesuit fathers preached to Hurons and Choctaws,
They prayed to be delivered from the vengeance of the squaws.
'Twas the women, not the warriors, turned those stark enthusiasts pale.
For the female of the species is more deadly than the male.

Man's timid heart is bursting with the things he must not say,
For the woman that God gave him isn't his to give away;
But when hunter meets with husband, each confirms the other's tale--
The female of the species is more deadly than the male.

Man, a bear in most relations--worm and savage otherwise,--
Man propounds negotiations, Man accepts a compromise.
Very rarely will he squarely push the logic of a fact
To its ultimate conclusion in unmitigated act.

Fear, or foolishness, impels him, ere he lay the wicked low,
To concede some form of trial even to his fiercest foe.
Mirth obscene diverts his anger--Doubt and Pity oft perplex
Him in dealing with an issue--to the scandal of The Sex!

But the Woman that God gave him, every fibre of her frame
Proves her launched for one sole issue, armed and engined for the same;
And to serve that single issue, lest the generations fail,
The female of the species must be deadlier than the male.

She who faces Death by torture for each life beneath her breast
May not deal in doubt or pity--must not swerve for fact or jest.
These be purely male diversions--not in these her honor dwells.
She the Other Law we live by, is that Law and nothing else.

She can bring no more to living than the powers that make her great  
As the Mother of the infant and the Mistress of the Mate.  
And when Babe and Man are lacking and she strides unclaimed to claim  
Her right as femme (and baron), her equipment is the same.  

She is wedded to convictions--in default of grosser ties;  
Her contentions are her children, Heaven help him who denies!--  
He will meet with no suave discussion, but the instant, white-hot, wild,  
Wakened female of the species warring as for spouse and child.  

Unprovoked and awful charges--even so the she-bear fights,  
Speech that drips, corrodes, and poisons--even so the cobra bites,  
Scientific vivisection of one nerve till it is raw  
And the victim writhes in anguish-- like the Jesuit with the squaw!  

So it comes that Man, the coward, when he gathers to confer  
With his fellow-braves in council, dare not leave a place for her  
Where, at war with Life and Conscience, he uplifts his erring hands  
To some God of Abstract Justice--which no woman understands.  

And Man knows it! Knows, moreover, that the Woman that God gave him  
Must command but may not govern--shall enthral but not enslave him.  
And she knows, because She warns him, and Her instincts never fail,  
That the Female of Her Species is more deadly than the Male.  

Rudyard Kipling

# My Prayer

Most people, if they had a choice, would probably rather be a leader than a follower. This is the case with me. I would rather be a leader than a follower. Just because there are more democrats than republicans in the United States or that there are more Catholics than there are Lutherans in the world does not mean to me that I should think like the majority do and join that particular political party or religion. (Perhaps my "herd-instinct" is not as strong as it should be.) In any case, my reasoning leads me to believe that there are many more ignorant people in the world than there are intelligent and I would rather be listed with the leaders than the followers. (Note that this does not mean that all leaders are better than all followers; and note also, that I didn't use the words "educated people than non-educated," because I have found out that education doesn't necessarily mean that there is a direct correlation between a person's level of education and his innate intelligence. We have all met people who were well-educated and yet were inherently stupid.

However, in my examination of "prayer", it is noted that on this earth there are millions of people who pray, whether within a recognized religion or without one. Virtually all cultures have a way of showing obeisance to a higher power and have been doing this since the beginning of recorded time, are doing it now, and will probably continue into the forseeable future.

This is a case where the masses, in my judgement, are correct. Why would the world's peoples "pray" since the beginning of time if it were not somehow beneficial to them.

We are not talking here of "organized" religion. Organized religions, in my humble opinion, are the same as corporations or any other power structure in the world, no different. They simply want what everone else wants, "wealth and power."

We are talking here of prayer and prayer only. It seems to me, that prayer is a very personal desire and activity between a person and his creator. It has nothing at all to do with man-made rituals, and dogma.

As I look back on my life, it is apparent, to me, that it is totally unnecessary to ask the Lord for anything, because as it says in the Bible, the Lord always knows what you need and what is best for you. If you believe this, and you are a good person, then it is so! You don't have to worry about anything! If you are in the Lord's hands and one of his deserving children then you have a feeling of inner peace and happiness that you cannot imagine until you experience it yourself.

After spending most of my life studying various philosophies and religions I asked myself what could I do to repay the Lord for watching over me through my slow and sometimes painful maturation. The only answer I could ever come up with to please him is to abide by the above rules and in doing so, be kind and loving to his children and creatures on this planet. Isn't that simple? Can you think of anything else that would please Him more? Then why not do it? It is very easy to do after a while. All it takes, like any other undertaking, is effort and practice.

The following is a little prayer which I am happy to share with you. It has been my companion for many, many years; is is said in the middle of the night, at the crack of dawn, while driving my car, while resting, working, in short, any time I feel like it. It just feels good to thank my Spiritual Father for all He has given us on this gorgeous little planet.

Dear Lord, my creator and creator of the universe. Thank you for letting me open up my eyes to start a new day in your honor and service. Thank you for loving me, guiding me and protecting me. Thank you for letting me live in harmony, health and happiness. Thank you, dear Lord for letting me progress spiritually on my path back to you. Thank you.........

You can make up your own prayer if you like or perhaps you have one already. Don't be afraid of overpraying. It is one of the things that is not harmful. No fear of overdosing!

# Natural Theology

## PRIMITIVE

I ate my fill of a whale that died  
And stranded after a month at sea. . .  
There is a pain in my inside.  
Why have the Gods afflicted me?  
Ow! I am purged till I am wraith!  
Wow! I am sick till I cannot see!  
What is the sense of Religion and Faith?  
Look how the Gods have afflicted me!

## PAGAN

How can the skin of rat or mouse hold  
Anything more than a common flea? . . .  
The burning plague has taken my household.  
Why have the Gods afflicted me?  
All my kith and kin are deceased,  
Though they were as good as good could be,  
I will out and batter the family priest,  
Because my Gods have afflicted me!

## MEDIEVAL

My privy and well drain into each other  
After the custom of Christendie. . .  
Fevers and fluxes are wasting my mother.  
Why has the Lord afflicted me?  
The Saints are helpless for all I offer--  
So are the clergy I used to fee.  
Henceforward I keep my cash in my coffer,  
Because the Lord has afflicted me.

## MATERIAL

I run eight hundred hens to the acre  
They die by dozens mysteriously. . . .  
I am more than doubtful concerning my Maker.  
Why has the Lord afflicted me?  
What a return for all my endeavor--  
Not to mention the L.S.D.!

I am an atheist now and for ever,
Because this God has afflicted me!

## PROGRESSIVE

Money spent on an Army or Fleet
Is homicidal lunacy. -
My son has been killed in the Mons retreat,
Why is the Lord afflicting me?
Why are murder, pillage and arson
And rape allowed by the Deity?
I will write to the times, deriding our parson
Because my God has afflicted me.

## CHORUS

We had a kettle: we let it leak:
Our not repairing it made it worse.
We haven't had any tea for a week. ...
The bottom is out of the universe!

## CONCLUSION

This was none of the good Lord's pleasure,
For the Spirit He breathed in Man is free;
But what comes after is measure for measure,
And not a God that afflicteth thee.
As was the sowing so the reaping
Is now and evermore shall be.
Thou art delivered to thine own keeping.
Only Thyself hath afflicted thee!

# Just Stories

There is an old saying, read many years ago and attributed to the American Indians. What tribe it was I long forgotten but the adage is the same today as it was then. It goes something like this--"Before you judge a man, walk in his moccasins for three days." This seems like a reasonable statement, doesn't it? So maybe before you get too far into this little book you ought to know something about its author. Perhaps some things that aren't generally known. Then you can tell better where I am coming from. I promise to keep them as short as possible and still get the main points across.

As a small boy, perhaps fourteen or fifteen years old, my parents saw fit one summer vacation to let me travel around the United States and see some of the famous sights for ten weeks. We had three stationwagons full of boys under the jurisdiction of our gym teacher, Mr. Perry Bean. At about the half-way point in our travels we reached the California coast, one afternoon. We were staying at a motel not far from a big boardwalk with ferris wheel, roller coaster, and other amusements. Mr. Bean told us that we could have the rest of the day off to do what we wanted to do.We were hot and fatigued from traveling, and standing on the boardwalk looking at the beach and beautiful breakers, it didn't take long to make up my mind as to what to do first.

After a quick change, it was straight into the water. The waves in this part of California were the biggest I had ever seen but as I had a lot of experience with smaller waves, I knew they shouldn't be dangerous if you dive into a swell as it approaches you and surface after it has passed. Not many people were in the water on this particular afternoon. There were only two others way down the beach and no lifeguard on duty.

The waves were huge swells and didn't break until they got near shore so I swam straight out intending to catch a big one and ride it in. Everything went fine until about the seventh or eighth swell. I looked up and saw this monster and then I remembered about, "Watch out for the seventh wave." A friend had warned me about the wave and suggested that one should count them to stay out of trouble. But his well-meaning advice had been forgotten. The trough between this wave was about nine feet from bottom of the trough to the peak. For some reason, this monster was already curling and I had no time to dive into it. As I think back, I know the Lord was with me because split second thinking (processing His ideas in seemingly slow motion with one hundred percent concentration) saved my life. I didn't want to get my back broken so I took a deep breath, tucked my legs up under me with my arms around my legs very tightly just as that towering breaker curled over me. Tons of water hit me and I went down and down spinning like a top. The water changed from clear and light to green, dark green and then black. The water was very cold down there. When I stopped spinning, it was so black that I didn't know which way to swim to go towards the surface. The thought came to me to let some bubbles out of my nose and see which way they go, and follow them. It worked! I could just see the bubbles in front of my eyes and the direction that they took so I followed them. The water became lighter and lighter until I could see the surface. It seemed about twenty or twenty-five feet above me. I broke the surface swallowing water, choking and gagging and decided that I had had enough swimming for the day. I caught the next wave and went ashore somewhat shaken. Noone had noticed my mishap and I never told anyone, but that experience helped me to grow up quicker than if it had never happened. Those ideas just came to me instantaneously and in the correct order. No damage was done physically, just to my ego. From that experience on,

through the rest of my life, I knew God was with me; loving me, guiding me, protecting me.

Incidentally, this illustrates one of the spiritual principles, one of the unwritten laws that you don't learn in grade school, prep. school, college or even Sunday school that I would like to share with you. It is simply this---Everytime you have an adverse condition happen to you, something that is painful or you can't understand why it happened to you, you will get at least equal payment in return for enduring it. Does this make sense to you? Do you understand? Every time something which you think is negative, bad, unnecessary (Lord---Why me?) happens to you, if you are a good person and believe that all things happen for the good to those who love the Lord, then you will learn something from the experience. You will be a happier, stronger, well adjusted, spiritual person because of it. And the reward is always much greater than the price paid.

Do you know something? As I look back on my life, I wouldn't want to change anything. I paid my dues and am happier now than if I never learned my lessons.
Unless you are a truly remarkable individual, you can't be happy with wealth. It is the spiritual things which are important. What a wonderful feeling it is to enjoy a balanced outlook on life, to realize that life is just a circus, a movie, something to go through and play your part as well as you can but don't take it too seriously.

# The Dive at Rowayton

One year, in my early twenties, two friends and I decided to go diving. It was sometime in the month of January and there was ice along the shoreline off the coast of Rowayton, Connecticut. We were on my thirty-one foot Chris Craft which was not taken out of the water that year.

We anchored in about fifteen feet of water at low tide and because I was running the boat, Tom and "Topper" jumped right in as soon as we anchored. By the time I had pulled on two sets of long underwear, two sets of socks, a "neck-entry" rubber dry suit, tank, weight belt, flippers, and mask, they had climbed up the boarding ladder and were getting undressed.

Let me explain about a rubber suit. When your lower extremities are immersed in water, the water presses the suit and all the air in its squeezed higher and higher as you immerse yourself until it leaks out alongside of your face. This, of course squeezes you rather tightly.

I jumped over the side and dropped into the water feet first. My weight belt was not adjusted and there were many more lead weights on it than I needed to make me "just neutral" in the water. The result, of course, was that I went straight to the bottom and fell over so that I was on my back in very cold water.

This presented some immediate problems that were frightening, if not terrifying. 1. My face mask had clouded over immediately and I couldn't see. This doesn't ordinarily present a problem because it is normally an easy maneuver to take your mask off under water, wash it, put it on again and blow the water out of it. But I found that the water had squeezed my rubber suit so tight that it was impossible to raise my arms at all. I could just barely bend them at the elbows, not nearly enough to reach my mask. 2. The cold water was giving me an instantaneous headache, the likes of which I couldn't believe. From the edge of the face opening on the rubber suit to the beginning of the face mask is a strip of bare flesh across my forehead, cheeks and chin which the near-freezing water was making very painful. Now it was understandable to me why Tom and "Topper" hadn't stayed in the water longer. 3. The guys on the boat were undressed now and it would take them quite a few minutes to get dressed in their rubber suits again, even if they were concerned about me, which they weren't. 4. One of the safety rules you learn now, when you take a diving course is to put your weight belt on last. In those days there were few diving books and no courses on diving to take. You just had to learn by yourself. When I went to unhook mine, it wouldn't unhook so I couldn't just stop "acting like an anchor." 5. If my diving companions eventually came looking for me, and I was still conscious, I would need air so I went to pull my reserve lever into the "on" position. No use! My arms couldn't bend that far.

"Well, Charlie, this is another fine mess you've gotten yourself into." You've got to find another interest; one that is more benign. If your wife ever found out about this, she would probably either: 1. Take a dim view of scuba diving or 2. encourage you to go diving more often.

What does one do now? It would be a perfect time to panic, but that wouldn't help the situation It is strange how, when you get into an adverse circumstance like this, how it seems to expand your intellect. It makes you feel powerful because you know that you are not just "fooling around." Your life depends on your decisions and mental discipline. Some people might pray and that would be fine if time allowed.

Lying there on my back, blind and uncomfortable, time seemed to stand still. You can think with, it seems, one hundred per cent concentration. No extraneous thoughts bother you, your mind doesn't wander. The thought came into my mind, Why not make like a flatfish or flounder as they are called also, and propel yourself across the bottom on your back and gradually increase your speed

and angle until you can point towards the surface. It worked! The water became lighter and lighter until I broke the surface. But where was the boat? There it is over there! My mask was fogged, but the boat was visible to me under a cold gray winter sky. I propelled myself towards the boat on my back "like a flounder" doing an occasional "three hundred and sixty" until I eventually grabbed the boarding ladder backwards and my companions helped me aboard. We decided to call it a day and head for home.

# The Foundry

It was about two o'clock on a summer afternoon. One of my duties, at the foundry where I was employed, required that supplies had to be ordered every week so that we wouldn't run out during the following week.

We broke automobile motor blocks by lifting an iron ball which weighed about twelve hundred pounds about fifty feet into the air until a rope attached to an arm tripped and the ball fell down on one or two motor blocks on a huge iron foundation buried in the ground. The pieces would then be small enough to be melted in our cupola. From the time the ball unhooks until it hits the motor blocks is approximately one second and during this time, the men that do this operation daily, hide behind the corner of the cement-block building.

On this particular afternoon, we were breaking motor blocks as usual for this time of day. I was checking supplies of limestone and steel and coke about thirty-five feet away with my back to the breaking area when I heard the warning, "watch out," followed by the click of the hook letting go of the ball. I turned my head to look but the ball hit the motor blocks as my head was turning. A piece of steel about eighteen inches long, six inches wide, and an inch thick came whirling through the air like the blade of a helicopter straight at my right shoulder. It could easily have decapitated me if it hit me in the neck. There was not time to think. My reaction was instantaneous, smooth and coordinated. My knees bent as I bent my body over and the piece of steel went hissing over me with probably nine inches to a foot to spare. "Yours truly" thought at the time that his body most certainly would have an inability to adjust to the sudden impact of "that" piece of steel. My father did tell me once that, "Working in a foundry is dirty, hot and dangerous." Over forty-three years, the veracity of this statement was confirmed on a daily basis.

About this time in my life, the feeling that the Lord was loving me, guiding me, and protecting me was becoming a daily part of my consciousness. Maybe He was saving my worthless hide for a reason. Only time will tell.

# The Mountain Road

It was springtime in the mountains of Germany. At the time I was attached to the Reconnaissance Company of the Forty-Third Infantry Division. We had been "rolling" since 04:30 that morning. The roads had been getting progressively worse as we got higher into the mountains. It had rained recently and the mud roads were very slippery. There were nine of us sitting in the box of a bouncing troop carrier called a "half-track." A "half-track" is nothing but a square steel box, open at the top, sitting over two large tracks such as a tank would have, and two wheels in the front to steer with. The column of vehicles wasn't moving faster than usual but the narrowness of the road coupled with the fact that there were no guard rails of any kind made you wonder what would happen if we were to slip. We came around a sharp bend and it happened! The "half-track skidded off the road to the right and over the cliff. Picture a right-angled cliff with our left track holding us and the troop carrier sitting approximately forty-five degrees. My seat was the last one on the right side farthest to the rear. The driver shut the motor off and we all froze. The Sargent yelled, "Don't anybody move!" Move--We were afraid to breathe! From my excellent vantage point I could turn my head ever-so-gently and look over my right shoulder straight down. I still remember it as if it happened yesterday. Little wisps of white clouds were drifting by about two hundred feet below and looking past the clouds to the foot of the mountain in the valley, you could see little fields with fences around them, cows in some of the fields, little houses, even a little, white church. It was beautiful but at the time, I kept wishing I were a bird.

After about twenty-five minutes, a "tank-retriever" came and put a cable on us.

Inch by inch we were pulled back up onto the road accompanied by cheers from a rather large audience of spectators that had gathered. First time in my life I felt like a hero.

It was an interesting experience. Talk about time going by slowly! Those twenty-five minutes have got to be the longest ones in my life. A lot goes on in your mind in a situation like that. It is a lesson. It teaches you to love life and be happy with what you have and don't worry about what you haven't got. Wouldn't trade it for anything. It was a good lesson.

# The Spot on My Lungs

One Thursday about ten years ago I had a bad cold, the usual symptoms but I felt real bad so I went to see Dr. Burke. He examined me and said that one of my lungs was full and he didn't like it. He sent me to the hospital for an x-ray and said he would call me the next day when he got the x-ray. He called me on the next day and said that I had a "spot" on my lungs and that I should see him on the following Monday.

Dodie asked me what Dr. Burke said and I told her, "You mean he said that you are not supposed to go in tomorrow? You are supposed to wait until Monday for an appointment? You're not going to do that. I'm going to call him right back." She did. Dr. Burke said he was going to bring the x-ray to the hospital that night and talk to the doctor whose job it is to evaluate x-rays. He did and the next day he called and had me get another x-ray. They taped a little square metal disk over my left nipple and took another x-ray. That afternoon he squeezed me in and showed me the x-rays. The second x-ray when superimposed over the original showed a small square of metal covering the spot on my chest. The technical name for what showed up in my first x-ray is 'nipple-shadow.'

This experience taught me to have even more faith than I had before. It definitely had an effect on my life for the better. It also had a profound effect on the life of my friend, "Poncho." When he asked me what the doctor said, I told him that the doctor said I had a spot on my lungs. He went out in the back yard where his friend "Flacco" was working and gave "Flacco" two packs of cigarettes. From that moment on "Poncho" never had another drink or another cigarette.

# The Story of Ung

1894

Once, on a glittering ice-field, ages and ages ago,
Ung, the maker of pictures, fashioned an image of snow.
Fashioned the form of a tribesman--gaily he whistled and sung,
Working the snow with his fingers. Read ye the story of Ung!
Pleased was his tribe with that image--came in their hundreds to scan--
Handled it, smelt it, and grunted: "Verily, this is a man!"
"Thus do we carry our lances--thus is a war-belt slung."
"Lo! it is even as we are. Glory and honour to Ung!"

Later he pictured an aurochs--later he pictured a bear--
Pictured the sabre-tooth tiger dragging a man to his lair--
Pictured the mountainous mammoth, hairy, abhorrent, alone--
Out of the love that he bore them, scriving them clearly on bone.

Swift came his tribe to behold them, peering and pushing and still--
Men of the berg-battered beaches, men of the boulder-hatched hill--
Hunters and fishers and trappers, presently whispering low:
"Yea, they are like--and it may be. But how does the Picture-man know?"
"Ung--hath he slept with the Aurochs--watched where the Mastodon roam?"
"Spoke on the ice with the Bow-head--followed the Sabre-tooth home?"
"Nay! These are toys of his fancy! If he have cheated us so,"
"How is there truth in his image--the man that he fashioned of snow?"

Wroth was that maker of pictures--hotly he answered the call:
"Hunters and fishers and trappers, children and fools are ye all!"
"Look at the beasts when ye hunt them!" Swift from the tumult he broke,
Ran to the cave of his father and told him the shame that they spoke.

And the father of Ung gave answer, that was old and wise in the craft,
Maker of pictures aforetime, he leaned on his lance and laughed
"If they could see as thou seest they would do what thou hast done,"
"And each man would make him a picture, and--what would become of my son?"

"There would be no pelts of the reindeer, flung down at thy cave for a gift,"
"Nor dole of the oily timber that comes on the Baltic drift;"
"No store of well-drilled needles, nor ouches of amber pale;"
"No new-cut tongues of the bison, nor meat of the stranded whale."

"Thou hast not toiled at the fishing when the sodden trammels freeze,"

"Nor worked the war-boats outward through the rush of the rock-staked seas,"
"Yet they bring thee fish and plunder--full meal and an easy bed--"
"And all for the sake of thy pictures." And Ung held down his head.

"Thou hast not stood to the Aurochs when the red snow reeks of the fight."
"Men have no time at the houghing to count his curls aright."
"And the heart of the hairy Mammoth, thou sayest, they do not see,"
"Yet they save it whole from the beaches and broil the best for thee."

"And now do they press to thy pictures, with opened mouth and eye,"
"And a little gift in the doorway, and the praises no gift can buy."
"But--sure they have doubted thy pictures, and that is a grievous stain--"
"Son that can see so clearly, return them their gifts again!"

And Ung looked down at his deerskins--their broad-tasseled bands--
And Ung drew forward his mittens and looked at his naked hands;
And he gloved himself and departed, and he heard his father behind:
"Son that can see so clearly, rejoice that thy tribe is blind!"

# Are We Done Forever, Mom?

Science of Mind - May 1978
A wondrous story of life and death.
by Beth Brown Tierney

"Are we done forever, Mom? Are we done forever?" Mary Ellen's voice, soft as an echo, penetrated through the quiet house. Before I could form a reply she had drifted back into her "other world."

Our six-year old daughter was dying of cancer. Reticulum cell lymphosarcoma was the technical name and the slides of tissue that we had been shown had a sort of wild beauty -- it was hard to believe that such treachery lurked in those cells.

Nine months had passed since that first biopsy and the ensuing cobalt treatments. She had spent several of those months in the wondrous world of first grade. She had learned to read avidly, as though suspecting that she might not have enough time to dip into all of those wonderful books.

Before Christmas, however, her body structure, which always had a sturdy, peasant quality, took on a more delicate appearance. An occasional trip to the hospital for a day of testing or a transfusion were our only outings. Fortunately for us our doctors agreed that we could make her more comfortable and secure at home, so we had very few hospital "overnights."

We did schoolwork at home after Christmas and it was a source of great pride to her when the teacher visited and informed us that Mary Ellen was working ahead of her class.

January and part of February were joyful and she lived as fully as possible -- from a wheelchair, to be sure -- although these months marked the beginning of a losing battle with pain.

Finally the time came when there wasn't much I could do for her except just to be there. So I sat beside her, and she was "safe" in her own familiar bed, surrounded by her books, gloomy old Eeyore from Winnie The Pooh, and her pet white mice, Fred and Milton.

I sat and prayed -- prayed that the end of her life on earth would not be frightening to her and that someone "there" would be waiting to take over my job, that was being terminated so prematurely.

Those last few days were a kaleidoscope. Mary Ellen, never at a loss for words, hovered between two worlds and had picturesque conversations in both! I soon learned to differentiate between the remarks that were meant for God and those meant for me. If, by chance, I intruded at the wrong time I received a polite "Mom, I wasn't talking to you!"

When she closed her eyes and started her other-world communication I jotted down much of her conversation, knowing how important the sharing of this experience would be to her father at work, and her sisters and brother at school.

Her talks with God were especially wondrous, as she was a very skeptical child. In fact, one of her first remarks to her "other-world" voice was "Are you really God? Well you'll have to show me!" Though she had no formal religious training, we had always acknowledged the presence of God in our home, but the acknowledgment came in the form of love and thoughtfulness we all shared,

not in terms of golden streets or winged angels. Therefore Mary Ellen had no preconceived images.

As the pain became increasingly hard to alleviate, one day she burst out, "Mom, I think God's a big phony!"

I did a double-take and then replied, "But think of our vacation trips -- the mountains and the forests and the ocean -- all of that beauty!"

She nodded. "Yes, He did all right with those things but be sure isn't doing much in the 'hurt' department." Half an hour later, this same little girl whispered in awe, "Is that an angel, God?" When I moved toward her, she again turned to me with, "I keep seeing things. I think I need a psychiatrist...do we have one, Mom?"

As the pain became rougher and we finally turned to codeine, we encountered a small problem. Shortly after her first pill, Mary Ellen flexed her little arms and legs, and sighed, "I forgot how good it feels not to hurt!" She then sternly fixed her eyes on mine and said, "Mom, I want you to promise that you won't give me any codeine until I ask for it. It feels good but it makes me 'fuzzy' and I have many things I want to think about, okay?" I nodded and kept that promise.

We learned to treasure those periods when codeine took over, before the fuzziness set in -- she knew her capacity and was not about to lose one precious moment of it, and I felt privileged to be sharing it.

One night, she murmured, "Oh, God, I think my back and neck are broken. I didn't think it would be so bad!" Another time she said, "This can't be infection -- it feels like splinters!" But each time I moved to get codeine, I was told in firm tones, "Mom, you made a promise. I'll tell you when I'm ready." During the last two days of her life, she would often doze for a few minutes, then murmur, "I wonder what's going on, Mom. Don't you wonder too?"

On the final day, she said, "What, God? How can I find anybody? Keep watching for what?" She repeated this several times, then said disgustedly, "Well, darnit, doesn't anyone understand me?" And later on, on another occasion, she smiled beautifully and said to someone in that other world, "It's real neat when you call me like that." How often I wished that I too could hear those voices and see those visions.

She was completely conscious for about an hour in the afternoon and discussed a family vacation we had taken in July, before we knew of her illness. All six of us had spent a month via train and car exploring the West Coast, from British Columbia, down to San Diego. It was the nearest thing to complete family fulfillment any of us shall ever experience, and she relived it that day. However, pain again swept into her body and she sighed, "I don't know about going on any more vacations, Mom. I feel carsick and seasick and airsick!"

This time even the codeine didn't seem to return her sense of well-being and she sighed into her pillow, "This sure isn't my day. I don't guess it ever will be my day."

That last evening, I sat by her bed. With the exception of her oldest sister, who was hurrying home from college, and her four-year-old brother who was asleep in the next room, the rest of the family sat quietly nearby, praying and listening. Mary Ellens voice came out in a breathless hurried manner -- not really talking to us but very aware of our presence. Once she murmured, "I want to stay long, please. Can I?" Then in the next breath, she said, "I'm never going to make it, Mom. You know that, don't you? I'm so tired and that's not healthy!" All of this with her eyes closed and not wanting an answer. Then suddenly she opened her eyes wide, looked up and said, "Who are you?" When I asked her what she had seen, her reply was, "I'm seeing things, all right, but it's a long

story."

Shortly after that she opened unseeing, glazed eyes and said, "Mom, I'm scared. I don't know why but I'm scared. Something strange is happening to me!" When I held her hand and told her not to worry, she gave me a reassuring smile and drifted off again.

A few minutes later, still holding my hand tightly, she reached the other little arm upward and whispered, "Mom, I'm going now. Mom, can you come with me? All the way?" With a tight voice I replied, "I'll try to stay right with you, honey..." With a small sigh, she let go of my hand and whispered, "Okay, Mom, I'll go on now. It's all right."

A few quiet breaths and she was gone into that other world where even mothers aren't allowed to follow at will.

We all felt as though the hand that had reached out to take her had touched each one of us. Our teenage daughter said with wonder in her voice, "Now I'll never be afraid to die!"

I silently thanked God for reaching to take Mary Ellen's hand from mine, then I thoughtfully answered that first poignant question of hers: "No Mary Ellen, we are surely not done forever."

# The Last Will and Testament of an Extremely Distinguished Dog

by  
Eugene O'Neill

I, Silverdene Emblem O"Neill (familiarly known to my family, friends and acquaintances as Blemie), because of the burden of my years and infirmities is heavy upon me, and I realize the end of my life is near, do hereby bury my last will and testament in the mind of my master. He will not know it is there until after I am dead. Then, remembering me in his loneliness, he will suddenly know of this testament,and I ask him to inscribe it as a memorial to me.

I have little in the way of material things to leave. Dogs are wiser than men. They do not set great store upon things. They do not waste their days hoarding property. They do not ruin their sleep worrying about how to keep the objects they have, and to obtain the objects they have not. There is nothing of value I have to bequeath except my love and my faith. These I leave to all those who have loved me, to my Master and Mistress, who I know will mourn me most, to Freeman who has been so good to me, to Cyn and Roy and Willie and Naomi and -- But if I should list all of those who have loved me it would force my Master to write a book. Perhaps it is vain of me to boast when I am so near death, which return all beasts and vanities to dust, but I have always been an extremely lovable dog.

I ask my Master and Mistress to remember me always, but do not grieve for me too long. In my life I have tried to be a comfort to them in time of sorrow, and a reason for added joy in their happiness. It is painful for me to think that even in death I should cause them pain. Let them remember that while no dog has had a happier life (and this I owe to their love and care for me), now that I have grown blind and deaf and lame, and even my sense of smell fails me so that a rabbit would be right under my nose and I might not know, my pride has sunk to a sick, bewildered humiliation. I feel life is taunting me with having over-lingered my welcome. It is time I said goodbye, before I become too sick a burden on myself and on those who love me. It will be sorrow to leave them, but not a sorrow to die. Dogs do not fear death as men do. We accept it as part of life, not as something alien and terrible which destroys life. What may come after death, who knows? I would like to believe with those of my fellow Dalmatians who are devout Mohammedans, that there is a Paradise where one is always young and full-bladdered; where all the day one dillies and dallies with an amorous multitude of houris, beautifully spotted; where jack rabbits that run fast but not too fast (like the houris) are as the sands of the desert; where each blissful hour is a mealtime; where in long evenings there are a million fireplaces with logs forever burning, and one curls oneself up and blinks into the flames and nods and dreams, remembering the old brave days on earth, and the love of one's Master and Mistress.

I am afraid this is too much for even a dog such as I am to expect. But peace, at last, is certain. Peace and long rest for weary old heart and head and limbs, and eternal sleep in the earth I have loved so well. Perhaps, after all, this is best.

One last request I earnestly make. I have heard my Mistress say, "When Blemie dies we must never have another dog. I love him so much I could never love another one." Now I would ask her,

for love of me, to have another. It would be a poor tribute to my memory never to have a dog again. What I would like to feel is that, having once had me in the family, now she can not live without a dog! I have never had a narrow jealous spirit. I have always held that most dogs are good (and one cat, the black one I have permitted to share the livingroom during the evenings, whose affection I have tolerated in a kindly spirit, and in sentimental moods, even reciprocated a trifle). Some dogs, of course, are better than others. Dalmatians, naturally, as everyone knows, are best. So I suggest a Dalmatian as my successor. He can hardly be as well bred or as well mannered or as distinguished and handsome as I was in my prime. My Master and Mistress must not ask the impossible. But he will do his best, I am sure, and even his inevitable defects will help by comparison to keep my memory green. To him I bequeath my collar and leash and my overcoat and raincoat, made to order in 1929 at Hermes in Paris. He can never wear them with the distinction I did, walking around the Place Vendome, or later along Park Avenue, all eyes fixed on me in admiration; but again I am sure he will do his utmost not to appear a mere gauche provincial dog. Here on the ranch, he may prove himself quite worthy of comparison, in some respects. He will, I presume, come closer to jack rabbits than I have been able to do in recent years. And, for all his faults, I hereby wish him the happiness I know will be his in my old home.

One last word of farewell, Dear Master and Mistress. Whenever you visit my grave, say to yourselves with regret but also with happiness in your hearts at the remembrance of my long happy life with you: "Here lies one who loved us and whom we loved." No matter how deep my sleep I shall hear you, and not all the power of death can keep my spirit from wagging a grateful tail.

# What is a Grandmother?

A grandmother is a combination of work-worn aged hands, after a lifetime of toil, a loving heart, and endless stories of the days when her family was young.

Grandmothers wear old age with dignity and composure. You can't notice what grandmothers wear, you only see the love and tenderness in her face as she fondles her youngest grandchild.

Grandmothers have run the whole gamut of human emotions, joy, defeat, success, failure, heartache, sorrow and perhaps tragedy, and have come through with the wisdom and tranquility endowed to those whose tears have been replaced by the calm acceptance and quiet outlook given only to those that have weathered life's battles.

# Mother, I'm Home

"Mother, where are you? I'm home!" Day after day, you hear that call. Over and over. When the littlest bounces in from kindergarten, proudly bearing his crayon drawing: "Mommy, here I am! Look what I made today! Mommy, I'm home!" At three o'clock, when the older ones begin to streak in: "Hey, I'm home!" Sometimes on weekends or holidays, the ones away at college: "I'm here! It's me! I'm home!"

And with that cry come both responsibility and rejoicing. As life begins to surge through the house, you take up the tasks it brings. The sandwiches they demand before tearing off to football practice, the money for the Cub Scout dues, the things to be found: "Honey, those shoes are right under the bed, where you left them." The phone calls: "Mary wonders if Jeanie can stay awhile."

And the day's adventures to be listened to, its triumphs and disasters: "I made it, I made it, I'm a cheerleader!" "Mom, Miss Johnson promised I could wash the board, but she chose Marie." "Mother, I've just got to talk to you about this boy."

It's a signal that peace is ended, that cry "I'm home." With the banging of the door, your day is stirred once again to action. No longer are you your own person. You belong to them.

Yet, in the confidence of that cry, you feel a surge of pride. They want you: they seek you out. However poorly equipped you feel for the job at hand, at least you're available and willing, and to them you're invaluable.

"Mother, I'm home!" Oh the ego in that announcement! Oh the glorious awareness of love! "How important I am," it seems to say, and you laugh sometimes at its brashness. But your heart is tender, too, even as you realize that they take you for granted---the fact of your presence and your delight in their presence.

"I'm home." They rap softly on your door at night, tiptoe in. "You can go to sleep now Mother. I'm home." And oh, the relief of that voice, the comfort of that good-night kiss, for the long vigil is ended, the hours of worrying. They're safe; the last one's in.

They grow up so fast; they go away one by one. After a while, only on their visits does that glad cry come. Hectic visits, filled with their outside concerns--dates, parties, or the turmoil of families of their own. The cribs are put up, the high chairs produced, and you know that you are no longer the center and hub of their existence, no matter how joyously they proclaim their own homecoming, bursting in. Home is somewhere else. A different job, a different life, a different love to follow yours, a different person to greet them when they return.

And that once-familiar cry has taken on a new significance. It means that you don't have to watch the clock any more when they're late. You don't have to worry. They have reached their destination. Each one is safely in. In a new and much more wonderful way, each voice is assuring you: "I'm home, Mother. I'm home!"

Marjorie Holmes

There is a paragraph Bruce Barton wrote many years ago that expresses a great truth: "As one grows older in fishing, even as one grows older in living, there comes the same consoling truth--that one need not catch big fish in order to be happy; that the spirit of the fishing is more important than the catch; that he who fishes well must fish with a calm and tranquil soul, drawing his reward from the joy of his fishing rather than from the weight of his fish.

Henry Ford liked to ride a bicycle; Andrew Carnegie's favorite hobby was listening to organ music; Edison played parchesi; William Randolph Hearst liked to go window shopping. We can begin living like millionaires right now, today!

Old-time Kings would have looked upon men flying through the air as gods, yet it is commonplace for us. Candles threw a faint light compared with the brilliance of the electric lighting we enjoy today. Kings had gold, but little else. The miracles worked with money are what count!

The most valuable riches of all cannot be measured by any material standard. The world's greatest thinkers are at our command to pour the treasures of their wisdom into our minds. One way to live many lives, during one lifetime, is to read biography and autobiography. To see the beauties of nature we need but to open our eyes. # When a Great Man "fails"...

A young scientist was confronted by a problem for which he could find no answer in reference books or the experience of his associates. # Were You Born Before 1945?

If you were born before 1945, You are a survivor! Just think about all the changes you have seen during your lifetime.

You were born before television, before penicillin, before polio shots, frozen foods, Xerox, contact lenses, Frisbees and the Pill.

You were before radar, credit cards, split atoms, laser beams and ballpoint pens. You were before pantyhose, dishwashers, clothes dryers, electric blankets, air conditioners, drip-dry clothes and before man walked on the Moon.

You got married first and then lived together. Closets were for clothes, not "coming out." Bunnies were small rabbits, and rabbits were not Volkswagens. Designer jeans were scheming girls named Jean or Jeanne, and having a meaningful relationship meant getting along with your cousins.

Fast food was what you ate during Lent, and Outer Space was the back of the movie theater. "Made in Japan" meant junk and the term "making out" referred to how you did on an exam. Pizza, McDonald's and instant coffee were unheard of.

You were before househusbands, gay rights, computer dating, dual careers and commuter marriages. You were before daycare centers, group therapy and nursing homes. Before 1945, you never heard of FM radio, tape decks, electric typewriters, artificial hearts, word processors, yogurt and gays wearing earrings.

You certainly were not before the difference between the sexes was discovered, but you were before the sex change; you made do with what you had. And you were the last generation to think you needed a husband to have a baby.

Time-sharing meant togetherness, not computers or condominiums; a "chip" meant a piece of wood; hardware meant hardware, and software wasn't even a word.

You hit the scene when five and 10 cent-stores sold things for five and 10 cents. For a nickel you could buy an ice cream cone, ride a street car, make a phone call, buy a Coke or enough stamps to mail one letter and two postcards. You could buy a new Chevy Coupe for $600 but who could afford one; a pity too, because gas was only 11 cents a gallon.

In your day cigarette smoking was fashionable, grass was mowed. Coke was a cold drink. Pot was something you cooked in. Rock music was a grandma's lullaby and Aids were helpers in the principal's office.

No wonder there is so much confusion and such a generation gap today. But, you survived. What

more reason do you need to celebrate?

# Diamonds

Spring comes a little later the farther north you are. At Mount Hermon Preparatory School, about fifteen miles north of Greenfield, which is about an hour's ride north from Springfield, Massachusetts, spring was right on schedule. The year was 1945 and school was going to close the next day for summer vacation.

There was a feeling of gaiety and partially suppressed excitement in the air in anticipation of going home to our "real home" the next day. We didn't expect to get much done on our last day of classes for the year. I remember the day very clearly; a day on which I would learn something that would affect my thinking for the rest of my life.

Jack Baldwin had returned from his duty in the Navy a few months ago. He was an average looking man, about five feet ten inches tall, black hair, muscular, and would be considered "handsome" from a woman's point of view I suppose. He was married to our German teacher who went by her maiden name Frau Donovan. She was a very sweet woman but also very strict. Jack Baldwin was also a teacher so when he returned, I was lucky enough to take his first semester since he got back. He taught economics.

On this spring morning in 1945, we all filed into class and took our seats. Jack was already standing by his desk in front of the blackboard. We were all watching him expectantly, we had learned that he was a good teacher like his wife. He too got his points across. He was young for a teacher and yet we looked up to him as if he were much older. Because he wasn't that much older than us, we could relate to him very easily; we felt almost as if he were one of us. Perhaps that was the reason we worked so hard for him. He looked at all of us and a hush fell over the classroom. Only an occasional birdcall would be heard through the open windows. From this point on I would like to give his farewell talk as if he were speaking in person. Although forty five years have elapsed, I still remember it perfectly. It made sense then; it makes sense now.

> "Good morning, class.---This morning we're going to do something a little different. Tomorrow is graduation day and you people will be scattering to all points of the United States and some of you to your own countries where you will all have a good summer vacation and then continue on to college, I hope.
>
> I will probably never see any of you again and that makes me a little sad because you have been good students and I have grown to know and like each one of you. Therefore, I want to give you something to take with you to remember me by: something very important, in fact so important that it can change your lives if you let it.
>
> When you leave here, it won't be many years until you have forgotten most of what you have learned of your subjects. You will, over time forget the room numbers, teachers names, and eventually even most of the subject names you have taken in the last four years. Be that as it may, I want to give you something to take with you that I don't want you to ever forget. Take it, think about it try it, use it daily and if it works, let it change your life for the better.
>
> Think of your life, at this point, as a diamond; rough, uncut, unpolished, in other words, "in-the raw." Now, everytime you learn to master something, or to like something, you polish a facet on this diamond which is your life. The more things that you like to eat, enjoy, do, partake in, makes your diamond sparkle more. Don't be satisfied with a dull, drab diamond, live, enjoy, learn to

everything you can; the more the better. Remember, each time you make an effort to like something,
you polish a facet on your diamond and your life will sparkle more.-----That's it. If you forget
everything else you have learned about economics, please don't forget this. It is my gift to you. There
won't be any class today. I want to say goodbye to each of you and may God bless you in your
endeavors."

# I Remembered

Have you ever wondered

what lies beyond this life?

And what about Reincarnation?

by

Merle A. Allison, F.R.C.

There is so much talk these days about life after death, so much medical questioning and hypnotic probing that not only the skeptical laymen is beginning to think about it and wonder, but the heretofore closed minds of the scientific professions are looking for openings into the study of this world of the Great Beyond.

Never before has there been such a search and it leads one to wonder if any credence would be given to an experience that deals strictly with a psychic phenomena concerning life after death—an experience that occured without the aid of drugs or hypnotic suggestions of any kind.

I cannot prove in any way that I relate is true in the sense of actuality, only that it is true for me. By this same token, no one can prove to me that it is not true. I did not dream this experience, nor could I, by the wildest stretch of imagination, have made it up. Experiences such as this are beyond the borders of the imagination. And then there are those who may claim it to be an hallucination.

The point of argument here is---the hallucinater expects everyone to believe his hallucinations, whereas I can only hope that my experience may cause you, the reader, to search a little deeper for the answers you may seek.

The experience was pleasant and in a strange way possessed an aura of mystery, for as it progressed, I was completely unaware of what was going to happen from one point to the next. All I knew was that I was completely imbued with a confidence of being protected from any harm.

As far as this world was concerned, it was behind me. To all conscious living persons, I was dead. But "dead" is a word used only by those who believe that one must be visible, and a breathing physical being to be alive. Rosicrucians call it transition and here transition was being proven to me; for in truth, I had made a complete transition.

Between myself and what I knew was the Earth from which I had so recently been parted, lay a dense fog---so thick that nothing was visible though it. Yet it blanketed me in a soft, comforting weightlessness into which I floated, at the moment, free of all restraints, all physical heaviness, all emotions but one: a strange ecstasy of freedom. Simply by thinking, I could propel myself up or down, forward or backward, in any direction I chose.

This new discovery was like a toy. It was like flying, only far better, for it required no physical exertion, and above all, the fear of falling was completely absent for there was no place to fall. I could float like a feather, without effort. And float I did, for there was nothing anywhere but the soft fluffy fog.

I call it fog, for there is nothing on Earth that more closely describes it; Yet it was not damp,

nor was it cold. There was no sense of either cold or heat, only weightless comfort and security.

But then a new element crept in. My mind, my thoughts were still as they had been, and I begin to question and wonder if this was all there was to the world beyond? Surely this nothingness could not be the answer. I grew troubled. This new-found freedom, this weightless floating was beautiful. But one could not float and do nothing forever, and here there was nothing to do but float---no place to go, no place to fall.

I thought: "Is it possible this is the condition existing for those supposedly `earth-bound`? What a hell this would be, to have nothing to do for all eternity." I simply couldn't believe this was all there was. The Great Almighty could not could not have created man only to consign him to an eternity in which he floated like a piece of flotsam. To make sense, there had to be more than this, but what does one do in all this fog, where does one go when there is no place to go?

I stared into the fog, willing, demanding that it give me an answer, and in the next moment I thought it was doing just that! But the voice that answered came like a beacon, from somewhere high over my head through the fog. The voice was soft, but commanding: "Keep rising until the fog is gone." The voice spoke only once and no more.

## THE LIGHT

Willing myself into what seemed to be an upward motion, I began to move slowly toward the direction from which the voice had seemed to come. As I rose, the fog appeared to grow thinner and as it thinned, little sparkles of light began to filter through the heavy gray blanket.

Suddenly and without warning, I seemed to burst into a brilliant light that stretched into infinity. Here was beginning without end. The fog was gone. Where it went, I don't know. I felt as though I had gone through some kind of time dimension. And flooding through me was a divine love of such a divine nature, that I felt in moments I would explode into a million minute particles of active light, each one radiating and vibrating with a love that transcended all love; a love experienced only by one who had reached this level of transition. It was heavenly in all the essence of the meaning of heaven, and it seemed to impart into my consciousness the idea that if I could sustain this glory very long, I would soon possess the power to create, as God himself created when he conceived man in his magnificent soul image. And so it was, in soul, that man was created in God's image.

I seemed to be drawn magnetically deeper and deeper into this tremendous light. What would happen next? What more could happen? The ecstasy was so terrific I wondered how much longer I could sustain it; and then the moment came, instantly without warning. From the depths of myself, I flared outwardly until I blazed like a comet, and I knew the greatest transition of all had happened to me. I, myself, had become a light.

Time ceased. Another dimension had been entered. Here I learned there were many who, like myself, had been transformed into lights; all a part of and glowing within, the greatest light; all learning, all growing and evolving to a higher plane of consciousness. A very few of these beings of light were being trained for dimensions beyond this one. There are dimensions beyond the comprehension of man; dimensions of different laws and different principles, of different aspects of life as it would exist within a more evolved soul personality. More than this was not for me to know, and I could remain for only a short while.

Though I prayed I would not have to return to my world, I knew I was not capable of handling the great mission that was for those who would never again reincarnate on this small Earth of ours. And I remembered the fog wherein I had learned how worthless life would be with nothing to do.

And the moment came when I had to return. I seemed to lapse into a state of forgetfulness and sleep. How long it lasted, if one can count time where there is no time, I do not know. When I awakened, all was dark around me, but I became conscious of three other personalities. And though I was aware of these three, they seemed not to be interested in me, but in the scene they were watching. Yet I had the feeling that their watchfulness had something to do with me--also that their cosmic mission was to give protection to those who believed that such was possible.

Far below upon the Earth's surface, in a tiny house, in a small bedroom, a child was being born. I watched for some time, unable to quiet the rebellion arising within me against what I knew was going to happen. For the first time, I knew what the next step would be. This unborn child was me--or was soon to be me. I was attached to it. In consciousness I struggled desperately against the pull. I could no help the struggle for I remembered too well the glory of the light I had been.

A voice from somewhere spoke within myself. "You must return to Earth," it said, not commandingly, but this time sympathetically as though it understood my grief in having to leave the world of the Great Beyond. "You still have work to do and much to learn before you can return to us, but remember, if ever you need help, you now know how to cross the gap."

The three personalities beyond me were conversing mentally, "How strange, that children must be born in such a manner," they agreed amongst themselves. "We can create our children mentally," There was a time I would not have understood what they meant. How I wished I did not have to be born of the flesh. These personalities could never be explained to anyone else. They were of a world beyond that point of "no return." But I understood them and I knew that sometime, somewhere, I would be one of them.

I turned once more to the scene of birth. The moment was here. The child was entering the world. I watched, it seemed an eternity, waiting almost fearfully for the moment. I saw the doctor pick the child up by the heels and slap it hard. It gasped and screamed as it took its first breath of air--and I remembered no more.

If you are one who doubt the idea of reincarnation, yet believes in a life of some kind, somewhere, after this one, is it so difficult to believe this life we live now is not the life after our last one?

In the Song of Bernadette, it is stated so beautifully:

> To those who understood,  
> no explanation is necessary---  
> To those who do not understand,  
> no explanation is possible.

You may call it fantasy if it pleases you, but I remembered.

The Rosicrucian Digest  
September, 1977

# A Hunter's Poem

A hunter shot at a flock of geese  
That flew within his reach.  
Two were stopped in their rapid flight  
And fell on the sandy beach.  

The male bird lay at the water's edge  
And just before he died  
He faintly called to his wounded mate  
And she dragged herself to his side.  

She bent her head and crooned to him  
In a way distressed and wild  
Caressing her one and only mate  
As a mother would a child.  

Then covering him with her broken wing  
And gasping with failing breath  
She laid her head against his breast  
A feeble honk...then death.  

This story is true though crudely told  
I was the man in this case.  
I stood knee deep in snow and cold  
And the hot tears burned my face.  

I buried the birds in the sand where they lay  
Wrapped in my hunting coat  
And I threw my gun and belt in the bay  
When I crossed in the open boat.  

Hunters will call me a right poor sport  
And scoff at the thing I did.  
But that day something broke in my heart  
And shoot again? God forbid!

Lemuel T. Ward  
Crisfield, Md.

# We're in God's Hand

Trapped 18 days in their car by a Sierra snowstorm, Ken and Jean Chaney left behind a diary of love and faith as a legacy for their children and grandchildren.

Friday, March 1, 1991, 6:30 A.M. Well, here we are in a winter wonderland. We have been here since about 6 or 6:30 last night. We skidded into a snowdrift on the wrong side of the road and couldn't get out. And then it snowed about another foot during the night. I can't even get my door open. (Don't mind the writing -- I have to write on my hand and lap...)

There was an intentionally upbeat tone to the diary kept by Jean Chaney, 68, as she and her husband Ken, 75, saw dawn after spending a night trapped inside their snowbound car in california's Sierra Nevadas. She seemed to know from the beginning that they were not in a winter wonderland -- they were sealed inside a tomb that would claim their lives 18 days later. But Jean Chaney wanted her last words to sound lighthearted, like a brave postcard. She wrote on the first day:

So many things I want to say. I want you all to enjoy your life and remember that what is so dreadful today will be forgotten next year. Please be a family!! And let my grandchildren know that I love them...

It was such an unexpected calamity, the result of a routine trip from the Chaney's home in Mariposa County to Fresno, 60 miles away, to clear up a tax question. On the way home, they got lost. After their 1984 Thunderbird piled into the snow bank, the devout Christian couple started writing on scraps of paper or the backs of envelopes.

We began to realize that we were on a road that isn't maintained during the winter. Truly a miracle if anyone comes by. We spent the night singing hymns...and quoting Bible verses and catnapping. We would run the heater for about five minutes every couple of hours...We have no idea what lies ahead...so here we are, completely and utterly in God's hand!! What better place to be!!!

In all, the Chaneys were missing for eight weeks. Family and friend had long since given up hope of finding them alive. On May 1, a Forest Service employee gauging snow depths in the remote mountain area -- 50 miles from the nearest town, North Fork -- found the car after the spring thaw. Jayne Peterson, 29, the couple's daughter, and her husband Karl, 32, a construction worker were stunned by the contents of the diary. Among the jottings were funeral instructions, a will and the record of her parent's final days.

The third day, and so far we aren't hungry. Found two little packages of jelly and a stick of gum in the glove compartment. Saving them. We reach out the window and eat snow. Daddy is feeling bad about not showing up at work this morning....

Ironically, Ken Chaney moved to California from Ohio to get away from snow. He was a high-school athlete in basketball and track who played triple-A baseball into his 30s. Until he was stricken with gout, he earned his living as a carpet layer. "Be sure to learn a trade," he told his son Skip, 33, an electrician. A powerful 6'1" man, he reminded people of John Wayne, with his good nature and blustery bad jokes. ("When someone said, 'Pleased to meet you,' he's always say, 'The pleasure's all yours,'" says his son).

Ken was a divorced father of three when he met Jean Wright in Goshen, Ohio. They began their ardent religious and charitable work after moving to California. They often brought drug addicts and the homeless to their house for meals, and with their children-- Madge, 37, Jayne and Skip -- spent weekends at migrant labor camps, distributing food and clothing.

Monday, March 4, It is pouring rain....We're wondering if anybody has missed us yet. We thought that maybe there would be helicopters or snowmobiles out looking....I wish I had more paper. I would like to write to each of you individually.

In 1985, the Chaneys moved to Antelope Valley, a high desert area 50 miles northeast of Los Angeles. They supported themselves by managing other people's properties, including a horse ranch. Ken was about to start a new job in a hardware store in Mariposa when he and Jean vanished. "He was always a good, kind man, but he became sweeter as he got older," says Jayne. If Ken grew into gentleness, it seemed to come naturally to Jean. "If you met her once, she would always remember you in her prayers," says Skip.

March 6, Wednesday. This will be our seventh night here. The gas is all gone, so no more heat. We have eaten our little packet of jelly between us, Rolaids and Tic-Tacs. Quite a feast!!

The cold ahd frozen the windows and for warter, they scraped the frost off the glass.

March 12. A drink of water will never go unappreciated again. And a bite of food -- any kind....Today is the first day that I have noticed any weakness. I love you all....

That was the same day that Jayne and Karl chartered a helicopter for $700 and conducted a 2-1/2 hour search of the roads around Mariposa. They looked nowhere near the stranded car.

Kids: I can't find the dome light -- writing by glove compartment light..Dad went to the Lord at 7:30 this evening, March 18. It was so peaceful, I didn't even know he left. The last thing I heard him say was, "Thank the Lord." I think I'll be with him soon....So much to say and so little time. I can't see. Bye. I love you.

There were requests for favorite verses and hymns at the services, but what the six children, 23 grandchildren and 28 great-grandchildren will remember above all else are the tender words left in the diary.

"We're fortunate that Mom was so sweet that she would give us something so beautiful," says Skip.
