# A Dog's Prayer

Treat me kindly, my beloved master, for no heart in the world is more grateful for kindness than the loving heart of me.

Do not break my spirit with a stick, for though I should lick your hand between the blows, your patience and understanding will more quickly teach me the things you would have me do.

Speak to me often, for your voice is the world's greatest music, as you must know by the fierce wagging of my tail when your footstep falls on my waiting ear.

When it is cold and wet, please take me inside, for now I am a domesticated animal, no longer used to bitter elements. And I ask no greater glory than the privilege of sitting at your feet, beside the hearth. Though, had you no home, I would follow you through ice and snow and then rest upon the softest pillow in the warmest home in all the land, for you are my God and I am your devoted worshipper.

Keep my pan filled with fresh water, for though I would not reproach you were it dry, I cannot tell you when I suffer thirst. Feed me clean food, that I may stay well, to romp and play and do your bidding, to walk by your side, and stand ready, willing and able to protect you with my life should your life be in danger.

And beloved master, should the great Master see fit to deprive me of my health or sight, do not turn me away from you. Rather hold me gently in your arms as skilled grant me the merciful boon of eternal rest---and I will leave you knowing with the last breath I drew, my fate was ever safest in your hands.

# Erich I

On January 20, 1975, the Aussenhofer family got a new member to the family, a thoroughbred German Shepherd puppy we named, "Erich." He was a remarkable puppy who, even as young as he was, showed more "promise" than any other dog I had ever owned. He was eight weeks old when we brought him home to his new family.

This is a true story and all the relevant facts are accurate. There has never been an explanation for what happened. It still remains a mystery, but this story proves, to me at least, that there is still much we don't understand and can't explain in our so-called "normal" lives.

---

This day started out just like any other ordinary "working day." The date was March 16, 1975. The weather had changed from the cold spell which we had been having, and the past two days were decidedly warmer, at least in the afternoons when the temperature had risen above freezing for most of the afternoons.

After playing with the puppy, starting off the day with laughter, chuckles and smiles and a hasty breakfast, I started off to work, which was only six miles away.

Since the day we got Erich, he had been coming to work with me each day and spending the day with me in the office. The office girls and foremen thought he was cute and played with him once in a while. But this day he would not be coming with me. He had to stay home because my wife and I thought it would be best for him. He had gotten some "Puppy Shots" the day before and the doctor told us that there might be some side effects. There was. He wasn't himself since he had the shots so Dodie and I thought it would be best if he stayed home this day and rested.

Driving to work, I smiled to myself, recalling that three days ago, on Sunday, it had been bitterly cold and the children had been skating on the ice in our swimming pool as the ice was about four inches thick. I had taken video movies of the children and Erich on the ice. The puppy had such a good time---he had never seen ice before and he wasn't very good at navigating around on it. The children weren't allowed in the pool area but because of the extended cold spell, we made an exception this day and allowed them to enjoy themselves. Otherwise, of course, the door to the six-foot wooden fence was shut and the children were forbidden to go in there.

It only takes about eleven minutes to get to work and soon I arrived and had to stop thinking of pleasant memories and start dealing with the never-ending daily problems, crises and decisions.

The morning went by uneventfully and before I knew it, noontime had arrived. As

was our custom in the office, we got a sandwich and coffee at the truck and spent half an hour or so chatting about everyday occurrences.

I remember the afternoon so distinctly as if it were yesterday. At about twenty-five minutes to one, I went into my office, sat down at my desk and started on some paper work that had been piling up. At exactly five minutes after one, I was sitting there working when I heard a voice say, "Charlie go home!" Now this voice was strange for a number of reasons: 1. It was heard in both ears at the same time as if the person speaking were right behind or above me. (Perhaps it would be more accurate to say that the voice was in my head.) 2. The voice was a male voice. 3. It was as young or younger than I was. 4. It was definitely a command but the voice was in a normal tone. 5. It was not a voice that I knew. The voice had no detectable accent. In other words, it was in perfect English but had absolutely no accent. I could not tell if the voice was from Maine, New York, The Bronx, Florida, Massachusetts, etc.

Now it was definitely not my custom to take an afternoon off and go home when I felt like it. There was no reason I couldn't take the afternoon off if I wanted to. The paperwork could wait, But what bothered me was, why should I take the afternoon off? There was no reason that I could think of so after pondering this strange occurrence for awhile, I went back to work.

At exactly three o'clock, I as was still sitting there, the same voice said, "Charlie, go home!" How strange. How could this be? What did it mean? Am I starting to hear things? Twice in one afternoon and just as plain as day. Should I go home after all? No, This is crazy. I'll keep on working as usual.

At exactly four-thirty as I was still sitting there working, the voice said again, "Charlie, go home! A persistent command but without raising the voice any louder. This was too much! I immediately made up my mind to heed the command and go home. I cleaned up my desk and was about to walk out into the outer office when my secretary buzzed me and told me that a salesman, a friend of many years, had requested to see me. I told her to send him in, as I wanted to be courteous to this friend. We talked for a while about the business and then he left. Anne, buzzed me again with a long-distance call. After the call, as I was preparing to go, she buzzed with another call. After finishing the call, I looked at my watch and the time was five of five, the usual time to go home anyway. So I rushed out and hurried home as fast as I could.

It was getting dark out as I pulled into my street and there, walking up and down in front of our mailbox was Jill, one of our twin girls. I stopped alongside of her and she rushed over to the car window. "Daddy, we can't find Erich. We were playing with him in the back yard and we all went in and forgot him outside." I hastily parked the car in the driveway and Jill said to me, "Daddy, the door to the pool was open and I looked in and think I saw something in the water." I rushed to the pool and sure enough, the door to the fence was open about eight inches. Somehow, the wind had blown it open. I opened the door and looked in. You could see where Erich had jumped in, thinking that the four inches of slush on top was ice. Instead of landing on the ice, he had gone through the slush and swam from the middle of the pool, along the side and around to the diving board and out to the tip of the diving board. There he had swum in a three-foot circle until the cold

water had claimed his little life. , When I found him, only his rump was on the surface and his head and shoulders were under the slush. I pulled him out and his little tummy was still warm. My heart was broken. There never was a dog on earth that I loved more than this puppy. We had an affinity for each other.

The next day, about eight o'clock in the morning, it was raining---one of those sudden spring rains, the first of the year. A friend of mine named Stewart Clarke, took off work so that he could help me bury my puppy. We buried him in front of the diningroom picture window in the rain. It was one of the saddest days in my life.

Looking back, this playful little puppy had left his mark on my soul. He had eight weeks of happiness with his mother and his brothers and sisters and six weeks of happiness with is adopted family. Fourteen weeks is not long to spend on earth. I pray that there is a life hereafter for puppies to enjoy. Somehow, it doesn't seem like too much to ask for.

This experience had a profound effect on my life. What is done is done. Nothing can be changed. It is history. But from that day on, I believe beyond the shadow of a doubt, that there is a God; that God is constructive and loving and caring ( at least in my case ) and that God is always watching over me, and if I will but listen, He will help me.

So. it is too late to help little Erich, but on that day I swore to never let a thing like that happen again. I resolved to be quiet, and listen to my "inner voice" and do what it says. Over the past years, since then, it has worked like a charm. It has worked so well for me that I taught my closest friend to do the same thing, and guess what? It has worked many, many times for him also!

I still don't understand what happened on that day but I believe...............

# At Night I Dream of Dandelions

01/18/95 (13:21:27)

When I close my eyes and think of childhood summertimes, I remember how, as children, we would find joy in the simplest of things. We could pass the days watching clouds go by, seeing in them all the wonders of our imagination. I remember searching the shoreline for that perfect stone, the one that was flat enough to skip across the surface of a pond. Or running through fields picking dandelions. I can close my eyes and see the fields and lawns sprinkled with yellow dot of sunshine. How bright they were against the green background, stretching toward the sky welcoming the warmth of the summer sun.

Ah, the innocence of a child, to find so much joy in a little flower. Hold a dandelion under your chin, if your chin glows yellow, you like butter, or perhaps you are in love. Braid them into a rope and give them to someone special.

When a dandelion begins to seed, the real magic begins. The yellow fades away andthe top transforms into a cluster of miniature umbrellas. Pick the dandelion carefully and blow the umbrellas to the wind. Make a wish, make two wishes, even three. Make as many wishes as you'd like. Watch the delicate little umbrellas carry your wishes and dreams on the wind, to the place where wishes and dreams come true.

As we grow older, we begin to see life in a different way. We stop looking at the clouds with imaginative wonder. We forget how to skip the stone over the water. We see weeds where there was once a little flower

What happened to the dandelions? Where did that go? We stopped braiding them into ropes for that special someone. We forget about the yellow glow under our chin. We forget about the dandelion stem necklace. As we forget about the wishes and dreams carried away on the wind to the place where wishes and dreams come true.

Tonight, when you close your eyes, think of those childhood summertimes. Dream about the ponds where you skipped the stones across the water,and remember the clouds. Dream about the days when you watched them with the imaginative wonder of a child.

And tonight,DREAM OF DANDELIONS and the place where wishes and dreams come true.

Rick Newlin
